_about: Short 'why' lines for the workload pages (analysis/dashboard_summary.py). 'workloads' applies everywhere; 'device_notes' adds one line for a device glob + workload. Plain English, 1-2 lines, no code names. Only write what the data or a verified check supports.

workloads.B1: Each element is read and written once with almost no arithmetic, so memory speed sets the limit; sizes that fit in the cache can run faster than memory allows.
workloads.B2: Every grid cell reads and writes 19 values per step with little arithmetic, so memory speed sets the limit.
workloads.B3: Mostly streams the matrix from memory; the irregular (power-law) matrix reads the vector at scattered places, which wastes part of the memory bandwidth.
workloads.B4: Building a sparse result needs scattered memory accesses and bookkeeping, so it reaches only a small share of the memory limit on every machine.
workloads.C1: Matrix multiply reuses each value many times, so large matrices run close to the compute limit; small matrices are held back by start-up overhead.
workloads.C2: Mostly random-number generation and exponentials; there is no simple operation count, so speed is reported as simulated paths per second.
workloads.C3: Small filters do little arithmetic per pixel, so only part of the compute limit is reachable; larger filters do more work per pixel and get closer.
workloads.C4: An FFT passes over the whole array several times; sizes that fit in the cache run fastest.
workloads.C5: Dominated by exponentials and reads of each pixel's neighbourhood; there is no simple operation count, so speed is reported as pixels per second.
workloads.C6: Sorting is limited by moving data and comparing keys; inputs that no longer fit in the cache slow down.
workloads.C7: Each lookup jumps through the sorted keys; once the keys no longer fit in the cache, every step waits on memory.
workloads.C8: Processors use their built-in AES instructions; the GPU uses a table-based software kernel. 'Hardware crypto off' shows the processor without those instructions.
workloads.C9: Processors use their built-in SHA instructions; the GPU computes the hash in software. Short messages spend more time on per-message overhead.
workloads.S1: Many threads add to the same counters and must coordinate. Measured with PyTorch's built-in histogram functions (library-level, not hand-tuned code), so results reflect that library.
workloads.S2: Each batch must finish before the next can start, so the cost of synchronizing all cores (or the whole GPU) dominates at small batches.
workloads.A1: Generating each token reads all model weights from memory, so it is limited by memory speed; processing a prompt reuses the weights and is limited by compute.
workloads.GEMV: Each matrix value is used exactly once, so memory speed sets the limit; small sizes fit in the cache.

device_notes.text: On this AMD processor, Intel's math library runs mid-size one-dimensional transforms on a single core (checked on the machine), which explains the dip.
The memory limit here is the pure-read speed: this processor skips the usual extra read when it writes whole cache lines.
Only the 1-billion-parameter model fits in this GPU's 16 GB; token generation is replayed as a single recorded GPU program to avoid launch overhead.
Our own hand-written kernel is the fastest at almost every size on every machine: general-purpose neural-network libraries are not built for one small filter over a large image.
The datasheet assumes a 1.53 GHz clock; under its power limit this GPU ran matrix multiply at about 1.39 GHz, which explains most of the gap to the datasheet.
Our GPU kernel reads each message separately; a layout that interleaves messages might be faster (not yet tested).

The measured memory limit (125 GB/s) is 61% of the datasheet figure; the same value was measured in an earlier session, so it is stable, but the cause (for example how the memory is installed) is not yet known.

Caution: this earlier-script result is at 97–99% of the theoretical memory speed, which is unusually high (real memory systems usually reach 70–90%). The earlier script averaged its runs and did not check results, so treat it as an upper bound until it is re-measured with the final scripts. The memory may also run faster than the DDR4-2133 that CloudLab lists.

cpu_wins._about: One line shown on the CPU vs GPU page for each size where the CPU is faster. A workload may give 'cache' (CPU-side data fits in the cache) and 'memory' variants.

B1.cache: The data fits in the CPU's large cache, which is faster than the GPU's memory.
B1.memory: The CPU is faster at this size.

B2.cache: The data fits in the CPU's large cache, which is faster than the GPU's memory.
B2.memory: The CPU is faster at this size.

B3.cache: The data fits in the CPU's large cache, which is faster than the GPU's memory.
B3.memory: The CPU is faster at this size.

cpu_wins.C4: Too little work to keep the GPU busy; its start-up cost dominates.

C8.cache: The CPU has built-in AES instructions and this data fits in its cache; the GPU computes AES in software.
C8.memory: The CPU has built-in AES instructions; the GPU computes AES in software.

cpu_wins.C9: The CPU has built-in SHA instructions; the GPU computes SHA-256 in software.
cpu_wins.S1: Many GPU threads update the same few bins and have to take turns.
cpu_wins.S2: Every batch needs the whole GPU to synchronize, which costs more than a barrier among the CPU's cores.
cpu_wins.slow_fp64: This GPU does 64-bit maths at 1/64 of its 32-bit speed.
cpu_wins.default: The CPU is faster at this size.
